replies:
Good — I’ll run a mock interview for a financial analyst role. I’ll ask questions one at a time, score your answers on structure, evidence and specificity, give one concrete improvement, then ask the next question. Ready?

First question: "Tell me about yourself and why this role."

(Answer in 1–2 minutes as you would in the interview. After your answer I’ll score it and give feedback, then continue.)

Score: 2/10.

Quick notes (structure, evidence, specificity)
- Structure (1/3): you said the action but didn’t set the situation or task. Start with a 1-sentence context (what company/product or decision) then your task.
- Evidence (0/4): no measurable result. Add a concrete outcome (accuracy improvement, time saved, decision enabled).
- Specificity (1/3): name the model type, one or two drivers, tools (Excel/Power Query/Python) and what “check against comps” means (which comps, which metric).
Rewritten answer (STAR, 2–3 sentences)
"In my last role I was asked to forecast subscription revenue for a new product to support a go/no-go decision (Situation/Task). I built a three-statement model in [your skill] linking ARR, churn and new-logo growth, ran scenario and sensitivity analyses, and benchmarked margins to three public SaaS comps; the model tightened our revenue forecast range and allowed leadership to set a phased launch plan (Action/Result)."
One concrete improvement to make it stronger now
- Replace "tightened our revenue forecast range" with a number (for example, "reduced the forecast range width by 40%") or, if you don't have a measured number, say the concrete decision it enabled and who acted (e.g., "led the CFO to approve a phased launch").

Next question (when you're ready)
- Answer: "Walk me through a time you caught an error in a model."

You improved but still has gaps. Score: 5/10.

Why (brief)
- Structure (2/3): your answer now has a clear Situation/Task and Action, but the setup could be one tighter sentence naming the company or product and your role.
- Evidence (1/4): you described an outcome (tightened forecast) but didn’t give a number or the concrete decision taken; that keeps the impact vague.
- Specificity (2/3): good naming of drivers (ARR, churn, new-logo growth) and analyses (scenario, sensitivity) — add the tools you used ([your skill], Power Query, SQL, Python) and which comps/metrics you benchmarked.
What to change now (one edit)
- Add one concrete result line. Pick one to insert:
  - Percent: "reduced the forecast range width by [X]%."
  - Dollar: "narrowed expected revenue to $[Y]–$[Z]."
  - Decision: "this led the CFO to approve a phased launch and delay hires for Q3."
Rewrite with a placeholder you can fill (2–3 sentences)
"In my last role as [your title] at [company], I needed to forecast subscription revenue for a new product to advise a go/no-go decision. I built a three-statement model in [your skill] linking ARR, churn and new-logo growth, ran scenario and sensitivity analyses, and benchmarked margins to three public SaaS comps; the model narrowed our revenue forecast and enabled leadership to set a phased launch plan. As a result, I [pick one: reduced the forecast range width by X% / narrowed expected revenue to $Y–$Z / led the CFO to approve a phased launch and delay hires for Q3]."
Next step
- Fill the bracketed result (one short phrase) and I’ll score it again and give a one-line tweak to make it interview-ready.

replies: Saved: Knows SQL, Excel and Tableau; 2 years of reporting experience. Is that right?

Your draft fact matches well: SQL, Excel and Tableau plus 2 years reporting are core data-analyst skills. Specific matches and how employers read them:
- SQL — essential. Hiring teams expect querying, joins, aggregations, basic performance tuning, and ability to turn business questions into queries.
- Excel — essential. They expect pivot tables, lookup functions, data cleaning with formulas, and sometimes VBA or Power Query.
- Tableau — essential for visualization and dashboards; shows you can present findings and build interactive reports.
- 2 years of reporting experience — shows practical domain experience: building recurring reports, understanding KPIs, working with stakeholders and delivering actionable insights.
Gaps employers commonly look for (pick the top 1–2 to address next):
- Clear examples of outcomes and metrics (what improved because of your reports? % time saved? revenue or churn impact?).
- Any statistical or modeling skills (Python/R, A/B testing, regression) if the role asks for analysis beyond reporting.
- Data engineering or pipeline experience (ETL tools, dbt, Airflow) for roles that want ownership of data flow.

One next step: confirm the draft fact so I can use it in searches and tailored application materials. Shall I confirm it now?

You don't have any Lincoln International application or interview on file yet. The one step that starts that record is: paste or forward the interview invite (date, time, meeting format and who you'll meet) or tell me those details now so I can save it and make a brief.

Below is a focused last-round prep plan and the things we'll do now (I assumed you're interviewing for an analyst role in investment banking / M&A; tell me if the team is different).
1) What interviewers ask and why — 6 question types
- Fit / motivation: "Why Lincoln? Why investment banking?" They want commitment, understanding of the firm and cultural fit. Give a concise story tying your background to deal work and Lincoln’s mid-market focus.
- Behavioral / teamwork: STAR stories about teamwork, handling pressure, mistakes, and giving/receiving feedback.
- Technical accounting & modeling: walk-through an LBO, 3-statement linkage, working capital, and simple valuation (DCF comps precedent transactions). Expect drilled follow-ups.
- Deal experience / transaction walkthroughs: if you listed deals, be ready to explain your role, the timeline, key drivers, numbers and the outcome.
- Case / brainteaser or modeling test: a short on-the-spot model or valuation with limited info; structure your approach first, then compute.
- Questions for them: thoughtful queries about deal flow, typical analyst path, recent Lincoln deals, and what success looks like in year one.
2) Quick scripts (concise, useable in replies)
- Why Lincoln (30–45s): [One-sentence background] + "I want hands-on M&A experience working on mid-market cross-border deals" + "Lincoln’s focus on [sector if relevant], its global platform and reputation for analyst training make it the right place for me." Add one concrete Lincoln deal or fact if you can.
- Strengths (20–30s): state 2 skills (modeling + client communication or diligence), give one short example and the impact.
- Weakness / gap (30s): honest, show learning: "I had less exposure to pitchbooks early on, so I took an advanced modeling course and built 5 sample pitchbooks; now I lead the modeling for proposals."
3) Top technical refresh (study these now, with exact items to rehearse)
- Walk a 3-statement link: explain how an increase in sales flows to cash via net income → depreciation & changes in working capital → capex → cash flow from operations/investing.
- LBO mechanics: purchase price, equity vs debt, sources & uses, debt paydown, exit multiple, IRR calc (show simplified numbers).
- DCF quick: NOPAT, unlevered FCF, WACC (high-level), terminal value (exit multiple method), sensitivity to growth and multiple.
- Comps and precedent transactions: when you use each and how one deal feature (e.g., strategic buyer) changes multiples.
- Accounting gotchas: EBITDA vs cash flow, deferred revenue, one-time items.

4) Short list of behavioral stories to prepare (use STAR, 1–2 min each)
- A deal/transaction you worked on: your role, a challenge, what you did, result (numbers if possible).
- Time you fixed an error or improved a model under deadline.
- A team conflict you helped resolve.
- A time you learned a new skill quickly under pressure.
5) On-the-day tactics
- Ask for clarification on cases; outline your approach before calculating.
- If given a modeling task, talk through assumptions aloud; show structure first.
- Use concise answers; interviewers test clarity under time pressure.
- End with 2–3 tailored questions: recent Lincoln deal you read about, team’s typical deal responsibilities for analysts, and next steps/timeline.

6) 20-minute prep checklist (what to run through now)
- 5-minute pitch: practice your "Why Lincoln" and 30s background.
- 10-minute technical drills: walk a 3-statement link and LBO aloud.
- 5-minute behavioral run: say two STAR stories end-to-end.
7) Scoring and feedback plan (how I’ll help if you want)
- If you want mock Q/A: I’ll ask one behavioral or technical question now; you answer as you would in the interview; I’ll score structure, evidence, specificity and give one concrete fix, then ask the next. (We can do a 10-question mock run.)

Next step: Do you want a mock now (I’ll ask the first question), or would you rather I draft concise answers for your top 4 behavioral stories and the "Why Lincoln" pitch? One question: which would you prefer now — mock interview, or drafted answers to rehearse?
